title: 2×2 rib baby blanket
subtitle: An elastic DK blanket in 2×2 ribbing for a baby's cot.
excerpt: A 75 by 90 cm cot blanket worked flat in 2×2 rib on 4 mm needles, using about 260 g of machine-washable DK. The ribbing creates a fabric with far more elasticity than garter or stocking stitch, making the blanket easy to tuck in around a cot mattress.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 4th series (1888), §Babies' Woollen Wraps, lists ribbed baby blankets as a standard nursery pattern and recommends 2×2 rib over 1×1 rib for its greater warmth and body. Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870), §Knitting, §Ribbed Infant's Wrap, uses the same construction.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stitch pattern formed by knitting 2 stitches then purling 2 stitches across each row, and reversing them on the return row so the columns of knit and purl align vertically. Produces a fabric with strong elasticity that can stretch considerably widthwise and springs back when released.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle worked flat in
2×2 rib
on 4 mm needles, finishing at 75 cm wide by 90 cm long when measured slightly stretched.

A single panel requires no seaming and is simpler to launder than a blanket made from joined squares. 2×2 rib was chosen for its elasticity: the columns of knit and purl stitches allow the blanket to stretch considerably widthwise and tuck snugly around a cot mattress, which garter stitch cannot do. Note that ribbing pulls in widthwise when relaxed; the blanket will look narrower off the needle than the finished measurement, which assumes the rib is slightly stretched to its natural resting width. Budget about 260 g (about 570 m / 625 yards) of machine-washable DK. Buy all the yarn at once in matched dye lots.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 260 g (about 570 m / 625 yards) of DK-weight machine-washable yarn
items.substitutions: Superwash merino or superwash wool-cotton DK. Ribbing emphasises dye-lot differences slightly more than garter stitch; buy all skeins at once.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) straight or circular needle, 80 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 28 rows to 10 cm over 2×2 rib, slightly stretched, on 4 mm needles. Ribbing gauge must be measured with the swatch slightly spread widthwise to its natural resting position, not laid completely flat with no tension. The unstretched swatch will read about 18 stitches per 10 cm; pulled gently to its natural resting stretch, it reads about 22.

If your gauge is 20 stitches per 10 cm at slight stretch with a 164-stitch cast-on, the blanket will be about 82 cm wide. Adjust the cast-on to the nearest multiple of 4 (for the rib repeat) if you need a different width.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on
Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 164 stitches (a multiple of 4 for the 2×2 rib repeat). Long-tail tail: (4 × 164) / 10 + 15 = 65.6 + 15 = 81 cm. Measure 90 cm of tail.
Body
Every row (RS and WS): *k2, p2; repeat from * to end.

Because the stitch count is a multiple of 4, the row ends on p2 and both RS and WS rows use the same instruction. Work until the blanket measures 90 cm from the cast-on, measured with the rib slightly stretched to its natural resting width.
When you set this aside, note whether you are on a RS or WS row. Both rows begin k2. Noting the parity helps if you need to count rows later.
Stitch count check-ins

At row 126 (about 45 cm): count across. You should have 164 stitches. The count must be a multiple of 4; if it is not, find where the extra or missing stitch occurred and fix it before continuing. At row 250 (about 89 cm): count again before the final cast-off.
Common faults

Rib columns shifting by one stitch: the pattern starts the row on the wrong stitch. Check that the first two stitches are the same as the last row's first two stitches. If the blanket looks like a single-column shift, you have added or dropped a stitch and need to find and correct it.

Yarn-over between rib columns: the yarn was not moved between front (for purl) and back (for knit) correctly. Before each knit, move the yarn firmly to the back; before each purl, bring the yarn firmly to the front, passing under the needle.
Cast-off
Cast off in pattern (k the knits, p the purls), with a looser tension than feels natural. Ribbing cast-offs bind the top edge tightly and reduce the elasticity; work each stitch deliberately loose.
Finishing
Weave in both ends on the wrong side along rib columns for at least 5 cm each. Trim. A light wash and flat dry will relax any uneven tension rows and let the rib settle at its natural width.
Care
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle if the yarn label permits. Lay flat to dry; pulling the blanket into its ribbed width while damp. Do not tumble dry.
What to try next

From 2×2 rib, the natural progression is fisherman's rib: a 2×2 rib worked with a knit-1-below instead of a plain knit, which doubles the height of each rib column and produces a thicker, plushier fabric at the same needle size. The cast-on and instructions are nearly identical.
